text: In a circular orbit, gravity is the only force that provides the centripetal force for a satellite, therefore \(GMm/r^{2}=mv^{2}/r\), from which \(v=\sqrt{GM/r}\) is obtained. Thus the orbital speed is inversely related to the square root of the radius: a satellite that moves slowly in a circular orbit must be farther from Earth. Consequently, if the satellite’s speed decreases while it remains in a circular orbit, its orbital radius increases. Its period, \(T=2\pi r/v\), also increases, because the path becomes longer while the speed is lower; this matches Kepler’s third law, \(T^{2}\propto r^{3}\).
